conversation.content: What is REST and how is it different from GraphQL?

REST is a set of architectural conventions for HTTP APIs: resources are URLs, operations are HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE), responses are typically JSON. GraphQL is a query language for APIs: there's one endpoint, the client specifies exactly what fields it wants in the request, and the server returns exactly that shape. REST tends to over-fetch or under-fetch (you get the whole user object when you only needed the name). GraphQL solves that with precise queries but adds client complexity and server-side resolver overhead.

501(c)(3): no political campaign activity whatsoever (no endorsements, no donations to campaigns), lobbying is permitted but limited (substantial part test or 501(h) election). 501(c)(4): can engage in lobbying without limit, can do some political campaign activity as long as it's not the primary activity (the 'primary purpose' test is vague and contested). The key trade-off: (c)(3) status lets donors deduct contributions; (c)(4) contributions are not deductible. Most orgs run a (c)(3) and a (c)(4) in tandem.

Lean focuses on eliminating waste â€” anything that doesn't add value from the customer's perspective (excess inventory, waiting, overprocessing, defects, motion). Toyota Production System is the canonical example. Six Sigma focuses on reducing process variation and defects â€” it uses statistical methods (DMAIC) to drive defect rates toward 3.4 per million. They're complementary, not alternatives. Lean Sigma combines both: lean removes waste, Six Sigma reduces variation. Most manufacturers with serious quality requirements end up running both.

conversation.content: What's the actual difference between a data lake and a data lakehouse? My company is building on S3 and we keep having this terminology argument in design reviews.

Data lake: raw storage (S3, GCS) with files in any format â€” no ACID transactions, no schema enforcement, queries are slow and expensive because there's no indexing. Data lakehouse: adds a metadata+transaction layer (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) on top of the same object storage. You get ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and query optimization via metadata â€” essentially the benefits of a data warehouse without leaving your S3 bucket. If you're already on S3, adding Delta Lake or Iceberg on top of it is how you upgrade lake â†’ lakehouse.
